content: 1. A study conducted by Sinha et al. The findings were published in the Asia-Pacific Journal of Public Health in 2010. 2. Uejio et al. (2016) investigated the effects of high indoor temperatures on the self-perceived health of elderly individuals. This study was published in Indoor Air and highlighted the impact of environmental conditions on health outcomes. 3. Van Loenhout et al. (2016) explored the relationship between high indoor temperatures and self-perceived health among elderly individuals. The results were published in Environmental Research and emphasized the health risks associated with elevated indoor temperatures. 4. Chen et al. (2011) conducted a study involving 16 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 22 years in a climatic chamber. Participants were exposed to temperature changes, including step-downs from 32°C to 24°C and 28°C to 24°C, as well as a step-up from 20°C to 24°C. The study assessed thermal sensation and skin physiological properties, such as capillary blood flow, skin moisture, transepidermal water loss, and skin temperature. 5. Fang et al. (2004) studied 30 female subjects with an average age of 23 years in a controlled office environment. The study evaluated the effects of different ventilation rates and temperature-humidity combinations (20°C/40% RH, 23°C/50% RH, and 26°C/60% RH) on office productivity, thermal comfort, and symptoms of sick building syndrome. 6. Jin et al. (2011) examined 23 healthy volunteers under 29 different test conditions simulating summer and winter environments. The study assessed the impact of varying air velocities and nozzle positions around the head, with summer temperatures set at 24°C, 28°C, and 30°C. Thermal sensation, particularly at the head, was evaluated. 7. Liu et al. (2008) involved 33 healthy volunteers divided into three groups, each exposed to four different temperatures for 40 minutes. Group 1 experienced 21°C, 24°C, 26°C, and 29°C; Group 2 experienced 29°C, 26°C, 24°C, and 21°C; and Group 3 experienced 21°C, 28°C, 30°C, and 24°C. 8. A study in 2012 involved 12 men with a mean age of 72 years and chronic heart failure. 9. Another study in 2013 included 12 men with stable heart failure aged 46 to 90 years, along with a control group of six individuals (five men and one woman) with hypertension aged 51 to 75 years. 10. A study involving Indian participants aged 4 years was split into two parts with at least a half-day gap. The first part involved a conference room where the temperature decreased from 27°C to 21°C, while the second part involved a laboratory room where the temperature increased from 28°C to 33°C. 11. Another study isolated participants in a sealed housing unit for 30 days, exposing them to 1% relative humidity. 12. Schellen et al. (2010) studied 16 male healthy volunteers, including eight young adults (aged 22–25 years) and eight older adults (aged 67–73 years), in a climate chamber. Participants were exposed to two conditions for eight hours each: a steady-state temperature of 22.5°C and a transient state with temperatures drifting between 17°C and 25°C. 13. Another study involved participants in a climatic chamber set at three different temperatures (32°C, 36°C, and 40°C) and three levels of relative humidity, resulting in nine conditions. Participants completed light, moderate, and heavy work under each condition. 14. Tham (2004) studied 56 female customer service operators aged 25–36 years working in a call center. The study tested two air velocities and two temperatures (23°C and 26.5°C) in a factorial design. Thermal comfort, workers' talk time performance, and perceptions of sick building syndrome symptoms were evaluated.
